Miss Kenton leaves Darlington Hall to pursue what will end up as an unhappy marriage, and she tenderly and nostalgically reflects on what her life would have been like had she stayed at Darlington Hall in close proximity to Stevens. LORD DARLINGTON Lord Darlington is the owner of Darlington Hall and the former employer of Stevens and the rest of the staff in the interwar period. He is a tall, slender man in his mid-fifties. Lord Darlington is a symbol of tradition, and stands for the values of trust, honour and morality. We learn through Stevens’ writings that Lord Darlington fought for the alleviation of the punishment that was forced upon Germany following its defeat in World War I. Lord Darlington’s sympathy towards the Germans continued into the 1930s as he contributed to the appeasement of the Nazis, a decision that was based on a desire for peace but ended up being disastrously short-sighted. Lord Darlington is a character of high moral stature, but in the context of a hostile and dangerous international climate which requires savvy diplomacy, he is perhaps too enmeshed in the old traditional value system based on honour and trust. MR FARRADAY Mr Farraday is a wealthy American gentleman who at the outset of the novel has become the new proprietor of Darlington Hall and thus Stevens’ new employer. Mr Farraday offers a contrast to Stevens and Lord Darlington and the solidity of English ritual that they represent. For example, his more casual and informal manner of interacting with the staff, shown by his encouragement of Stevens to take off time for himself and his bantering with him over inappropriate topics, troubles Stevens. Mr Farraday marks the passage of the time and the emergence of a newer generation freed from the tight reins of traditional professionalism. ANALYSIS THE OLD AND THE NEW At the heart of Ishiguro’s text is the conflict between tradition and modernity, old and new. Stevens is an effective character through whom we can consider this conflict because he is a butler in a grand English house – a profession rooted in tradition which in today’s world strikes us as somewhat outdated. Writing in 1956, Stevens claims that the professionalism of the past is “almost impossible to find nowadays” (p. 9). The disappearance of professionalism that Stevens notes is representative of a wider general progression from a traditional society to a modern one. One of the ways that Ishiguro illustrates this transition is with reference to honour and loyalty. Just as Stevens believes that it is honourable to remain loyal to his employer Lord Darlington, Lord Darlington deems it morally sound to remain trustworthy to his German political associates. Lord Darlington’s confidence in the German nation facilitates the Nazis’ rise to power, and this is a clear error of judgement. During one of the international conferences hosted at Darlington Hall, an American gentleman named Mr Lewis accuses Darlington and his colleagues of being amateurs in the sphere of international affairs. He bitingly announces, “the days when you could act out of your noble instincts are over” (p. 102). Mr Lewis asserts that in the world in which they now find themselves, doing what is right does not necessarily mean doing what is noble and morally virtuous. In this way, Ishiguro presents the malfunctioning of a generation that places the values of honour and loyalty over those of retaliation, cunning negotiation and pragmatism. It is significant that Mr Lewis, an adversary of Lord Darlington, is from the USA. Another way in which Ishiguro presents the change in world society is through the division between the USA and the UK. Both of the American characters in the novel, Mr Lewis and Mr Farraday, present an opposition or contrast to the old-fashioned Lord Darlington, and thus we can associate the themes and values that these characters are associated with to the emerging modern world: realism, hard-headedness, informality, attachment to money, and so on. MEMORIES The Remains of the Day is structured in the form of a diary. The reader does not see the action unfold as it happens, but rather sees the events of the story through the window of Stevens’ memories. It is very important to acknowledge that all the episodes of the novel have passed through the filter of one character and that this shapes the way that the text presents itself. Stevens is an exceptionally cool, composed and rational character, and thus it is no surprise that the narrative is balanced, not paced too quickly, and logical in terms of the sequence of events that is narrated; the novel intersperses memories with descriptions of the present moment that complement one another in a perfectly balanced way. Stevens is also an emotionally complex character, and this is perhaps the most interesting facet of his character revealed by his narration. Given that Stevens places professionalism over the acknowledgement of his own emotions, at moments when he is emotionally susceptible, he refuses to express his grief and we only learn of it through the dialogue of other characters. For example, when his father falls ill, Stevens continues working and does not comment on it at all. The only way we learn that Stevens is sad is because Lord Darlington remarks “you look as though you’re crying” (p. 105). The refusal to mention his own feelings is a very effective way of showing how this character supresses his emotions, allowing their only manifestation to be involuntary (tears). LOVE AND PROFESSIONALISM Love and professionalism are two pivotal themes in this text because they offer a conflict. In Stevens’ world, there is not a shadow of a doubt that romantic pursuit runs contrary to being a professional.
